===Indianapolis Colts===
====2004====
As a rookie, Sanders played primarily as a backup safety and a special teams player. Though his season would be shortened by both foot and knee injuries, he had some good performances during the regular season; on November 14, he made 13 total tackles while returning a fumble recovery 37 yards for his first NFL touchdown against the Houston Texans during their week 10 matchup. He managed 9 tackles and a fumble recovery against the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] for week 8.

====2005–2006====
Sanders played only four games in the 2006 regular season due to a knee injury he suffered early. In those four games, he racked up 27 tackles. He was soon dubbed "''the Eraser''", due to his reckless and punishing hits on opposing players which prevented many of the big plays that the opposing teams might have otherwise made happen.  The Colts had the worst rushing defense in the NFL statistically, allowing at least 100 yards rushing in every game. During the playoffs, however, Sanders continued his comeback from injury, and breathed new life into the defense. With Sanders, the 2006 Colts had the second best run defense in the playoffs with only 73.3 rushing yards allowed per game. Sanders went on to help the Colts on the road to their victory in [[Super Bowl XLI]]. Sanders made a pivotal play in the AFC title game against the [[New England Patriots]].  With the Patriots looking to clinch the game with a first down with under three minutes to play and holding a 34–31 lead, Sanders dove in front of Patriots wide receiver [[Troy Brown]] and deflected the pass, forcing the Patriots to punt and giving [[Peyton Manning]] the chance to drive for the game-winning touchdown.

Sanders made several key plays in the Super Bowl against the Chicago Bears, forcing a fumble from running back [[Cedric Benson]] early in the game and intercepting quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] early in the 4th quarter after cornerback [[Kelvin Hayden]] intercepted Grossman on the previous drive with both picks helping seal the 29–17 win.

====2007: Defensive Player of the Year====
For the 2007 NFL season Sanders was named AFC Defensive Player of the Week for Week 2, following the 11 tackles and 2.5 sacks he recorded against division rival [[Tennessee Titans]] at Nashville. He was largely responsible for shutting down [[Vince Young]] at the end of the game, clinching the victory for the Colts 22–20. Sanders ended the year with 96 total tackles, 3.5 sacks, two interceptions and six pass deflections. With him in the lineup, the Colts again fielded one of the best pass defenses in the league while also leading a successful run stopping defense. Sanders was noted by coach Tony Dungy as a prototypical safety for his [[Tampa 2]] defense and became known for his coming down into the box on run support as a big factor in the Colts' run defense.

On December 28, 2007, Sanders was signed to a five-year, $37.5 million contract with $20 million guaranteed. At the time, the contract made him the highest paid safety in the history of the NFL.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/football/colts-make-sanders-highest-paid-safety-1.670437?ref=rss|title=Colts make Sanders highest paid safety|date=December 28, 2007|work=CBC Sports|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|access-date=June 6, 2008}}</ref>

On January 7, 2008, Sanders was named [[National Football League Defensive Player of the Year Award|AP Defensive Player of the Year]] for the 2007 NFL season, the first Colt to earn the award and only the fourth safety in NFL history to win it.  He earned 31 votes from a nationwide panel of 50 media members who regularly cover the NFL. With Sanders in the lineup, the Colts became stingier and more physical as Sanders played closer to the line of scrimmage. Sanders received much of the credit for the turnaround in Indy's soft defense, which saw its yards per carry average cut from 5.3 in 2006 to 3.8 in 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2008-01-07 |title=Colts' Sanders named NFL's top defensive player |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3185005 |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}}</ref>

====2008–2011====
Sanders was expected to start the 2008 training camp on the [[Physically Unable to Perform|PUP]] list, but general manager [[Bill Polian]] had stated that Sanders would come back in the middle of training camp. On August 24, Sanders made his 2008 debut, along with fellow injured teammate [[Dwight Freeney]] in the week 3 preseason matchup against the [[Buffalo Bills]].

On September 17, 2008, the Colts announced Bob Sanders would be out for the next 4–6 weeks because of a high ankle sprain. The injury occurred in the Colts' second game of the season against the [[Minnesota Vikings]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2008-09-17 |title=Colts' Sanders could miss 4-6 weeks with sprain |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3592643 |access-date=2025-08-03 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}}</ref> Sanders would be replaced by second-year safety [[Melvin Bullitt]].

Sanders made his return from the injury list, along with teammate [[Joseph Addai]], for the week 9 matchup against the Patriots. After a five-game absence, Sanders had a solid performance and helped hold the Patriots off in the last seconds with the game-sealing interception with 4 minutes to go in the 4th quarter, his first interception of the season. During the postgame press conference, Tony Dungy stated that Sanders was "physically, very [very] close to 100%" coming off of the ankle injury.

Sanders again missed time for the season, sitting out of the week 11 game versus the [[Houston Texans]], due to a knee injury apparently sustained the previous week against the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. The knee injury caused him to again miss time for the second consecutive week. Sanders' knee injuries came about by the cause of swelling, a condition that he experienced since a serious injury to his knee sidelined him during his rookie season.

After missing the last two games of the regular season, Sanders total game appearances amounted to six. In those six games, he collected 39 total tackles and one interception. Sanders played in the postseason but the Colts' season was cut short by the San Diego Chargers in their wild card playoff matchup, losing 23–17.

In 2009, Sanders started two games before being placed on [[Injured reserve list|injured reserve]] on November 6 with an arm injury. He recorded six tackles and one interception in his two games.

In 2010, Sanders exited the first game of the season with an injury. On September 14, 2010, it was reported that Sanders could possibly miss the entire season with a torn biceps tendon. On December 8, he was put on injured reserve, which ended his season.

On February 18, 2011, Sanders was released from the Colts after only playing nine total games in the previous three seasons. In a team statement he said, "I always will consider myself a Colt. I want to thank the fans also for their great support. They played a big part in making my seven years with the team very rewarding."{{citation needed|date=July 2016}}

===San Diego Chargers===
Sanders signed a one-year deal with the San Diego Chargers for the [[2011 San Diego Chargers season|2011 season]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/n/a/2011/07/26/sports/s203052D00.DTL |title=Chargers reach deals with veterans |work=Sfgate.com |date=July 26, 2011 |access-date=August 6, 2011}}{{dead link|date=February 2026|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> On September 28, 2011, he was placed on injured reserve (IR) due to swelling in his knee after playing the Patriots a couple of weeks earlier. It was the fourth season in a row Sanders ended the season on IR.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Williamson |first=Bill |date=September 28, 2011 |title=Bob Sanders' body betrays him again |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/afcwest/post?id=32939 |access-date=September 29, 2011 |work=ESPN.com}}</ref>

'''Robert Lewis Perryman Jr.''' (October 16, 1964 – February 23, 2023) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player.  He played [[college football]] as a [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] for the [[University of Michigan]] from 1983 to 1986.  He played professional football, principally as a fullback, in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for six seasons for the [[New England Patriots]] ([[1987 NFL season|1987]]–[[1990 NFL season|1990]]) and the [[Denver Broncos]] ([[1991 NFL season|1991]]–[[1992 NFL season|1992]]).  He gained 1,247 rushing yards at Michigan and 1,338 rushing yards in the NFL.

==Early life==
Perryman was born in [[Raleigh, North Carolina]], in 1964.  He played [[high school football]] at [[Bourne High School]] in [[Bourne, Massachusetts]].<ref name=PFR>{{cite web|title=Bob Perryman|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|accessdate=April 1, 2015|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/PerrBo00.htm}}</ref>

==University of Michigan==
Perryman enrolled at the [[University of Michigan]] in 1982 and played college football at the fullback position for head coach [[Bo Schembechler]]'s [[Michigan Wolverines football]] teams from 1983 to 1986.<ref name=Roster>{{cite web|title=All-Time Football Roster Database|publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library|accessdate=April 1, 2015|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/rosters/football.php}}</ref>  He scored three touchdowns in the 1984 season opener against the #1 ranked [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami Hurricanes]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Error-plagued Miami falls to Michigan|newspaper=Gainesville Sun|date=September 9, 1984|page=4F|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1320&dat=19840909&id=keZQAAAAIBAJ&sjid=lukDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6894,2567364&hl=en}}</ref>  He also rushed for 107 yards on 14 carries and scored two touchdowns against Hawaii in the final game of the 1986 season.<ref>{{cite news|title=Michigan runs past Rainbows|newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard|date=December 7, 1986|page=4B|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1310&dat=19861207&id=UvBVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=V-EDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6896,1611295&hl=en}}</ref> In four years at Michigan, Perryman totaled 1,247 rushing yards  and 14 touchdowns on 274 carries.  He also caught 20 passes for 199 yards and one receiving touchdown.<ref>{{cite web |title=Michigan Football Statistic Archive Query Page |publisher=University of Michigan |accessdate=April 1, 2015 |url=http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071112175906/http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |archivedate=November 12, 2007 }}(to retrieve career statistics, enter "perryman" in the box for the player's last name)</ref>

==Professional football==
Perryman was selected by the [[New England Patriots]] in the third round (79th overall pick) of the [[1987 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1987 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1987/draft.htm |access-date=2023-09-30 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played four years for the Patriots from 1987 to 1990, appearing in 49 games, including 38 games as a starter. He gained 1,294 rushing yards and scored nine touchdowns on 369 carries (3.5 yards per carry) for the Patriots. He also caught 64 passes for 430 yards while playing for the Patriots.<ref name=PFR/> Perryman, along with Patriots teammates [[Zeke Mowatt]] and [[Michael Timpson]], were fined by the NFL for alleged [[sexual harassment]] stemming from a [[locker room]] interview involving ''[[Boston Herald]]'' reporter [[Lisa Olson]] in September 1990.<ref>[https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F30614FB3E5A0C7B8EDDA80994D8494D81 Patriots and 3 Players Fined in Olson Incident], ''The New York Times'', November 28, 1990</ref>

After being released by the Patriots, Perryman signed with the [[Dallas Cowboys]] during the 1990 season but did not appear in any games.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bob Perryman|publisher=National Football League|work=nfl.com|accessdate=April 1, 2015|url=http://www.nfl.com/player/bobperryman/2502455/profile}}</ref>  Perryman concluded his NFL career with the [[Denver Broncos]] during the 1991 and 1992 NFL seasons. He appeared in 19 games for the Broncos (eight as a starter) and gained 44 yards on 24 carries.<ref name=PFR/>

'''Robert John Kuechenberg''' (October 14, 1947 – January 12, 2019) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Miami Dolphins]] for 14 seasons between [[1970 NFL season|1970]] and [[1983 NFL season|1983]], spending the [[1984 NFL season|1984 season]] on [[injured reserve]]. He was a mainstay in a line that included Hall of Famers [[Jim Langer]], [[Larry Little]], and [[Dwight Stephenson]] and played in six [[Pro Bowl]]s in the late 1970s and early 1980s. He was selected as one of the top 15 finalists for the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] from 2002 to 2006, and one of the top 17 finalists from 2007 to 2009, but missed the cut every year. He was inducted into the [[Miami Dolphins Honor Roll|Miami Dolphin's Honor Roll]] on December 15, 1995. He was the brother of the retired Chicago Bears linebacker [[Rudy Kuechenberg]].<ref name="Hamnik">{{cite web |last=Hamnik |first=Al |title=NFL great Bob Kuechenberg makes his point with White House snub |url=http://www.nwitimes.com/sports/columnists/al-hamnik/al-hamnik-nfl-great-bob-kuechenberg-makes-his-point-with/article_b6eee357-f702-5a16-aa8d-baed54417b0a.html |date=20 August 2013 |work=nwitimes.com |publisher=Times Media Company |access-date=20 August 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130824174444/http://www.nwitimes.com/sports/columnists/al-hamnik/al-hamnik-nfl-great-bob-kuechenberg-makes-his-point-with/article_b6eee357-f702-5a16-aa8d-baed54417b0a.html |archive-date=24 August 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Early life ==
Kuechenberg was born on October 14, 1947, in [[Gary, Indiana]] to Rudy and Marion Kuechenberg, and grew up in [[Hobart, Indiana]] (located about 10 minutes from Gary and 30 minutes/35–40 miles from Chicago<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of City {{!}} Hobart, IN - Official Website |url=https://www.cityofhobart.org/294/History-of-City |access-date=2024-11-18 |website=www.cityofhobart.org}}</ref>). He attended [[Hobart High School (Indiana)|Hobart High School]], and played football for the [[Hobart High School (Indiana)#Athletics|Hobart Brickies]] during high school. Kuechenberg called his father the toughest man he ever knew, and said his father had such occupations as iron worker, boxer, rodeo clown, and human cannonball. Kuechenberg himself would go on to play football with injuries that would have prevented most people from playing.<ref name="Slotnik-2019">{{Cite news |last=Slotnik |first=Daniel E. |date=January 16, 2019 |title=Bob Kuechenberg, 71, Dies; Gritty Guard With Champion Dolphins |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/01/16/obituaries/bob-kuechenberg-dead.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> Kuechenberg's older brother [[Rudy Kuechenberg|Rudy]] also attended Hobart High, would also become an NFL player, and they would be inducted together on June 23, 1996, into the [[Indiana Football Hall of Fame|Indiana Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=KUECHENBERG, RUDY |url=https://ifca-hof.org/inductee/kuechenberg-rudy/ |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=Indiana Football Hall of Fame |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Indiana Football Hall of Fame">{{Cite web |title=KUECHENBERG, BOB |url=https://ifca-hof.org/inductee/kuechenberg-bob/ |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=Indiana Football Hall of Fame |language=en-US}}</ref>

== College career ==
Kuechenberg attended college at the [[University of Notre Dame]], where he studied [[economics]], earning a [[Bachelor's degree]] in 1969. He played both the offensive and [[defensive line]]s for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish|Fighting Irish]], including offensive tackle and defensive tackle on Notre Dame's [[1966 NCAA University Division football rankings|1966 National Championship team]]. He was a starting offensive tackle on the 1966 team. In 1968, he was the Notre Dame Defensive Lineman of Year (the Monogram Club MVP<ref name="Notre Dame Fighting Irish - Official Athletics Website-2019">{{Cite web |date=2019-01-13 |title=Former Irish Lineman Bob Kuechenberg Dies at 71 |url=https://fightingirish.com/football-former-irish-lineman-bob-kuechenberg-dies-at-71/ |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=Notre Dame Fighting Irish - Official Athletics Website |language=en-US}}</ref>). In the same year, he was also an Honorable Mention All-American Defensive End. Kuechenberg played in the [[East–West Shrine Bowl|East-West]] and [[All-American Bowl]]s. In is combined junior and senior years, he had 18 tackles for loss, broke up six passes, and recovered two fumbles. In addition to football, Kuenchenberg was [[third baseman]] on school's baseball team.<ref name="Slotnik-2019"/><ref name="Indiana Football Hall of Fame" /><ref name="Notre Dame Fighting Irish - Official Athletics Website-2019" />

==Professional career==
Kuechenberg was drafted by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] as a fourth-round pick in the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]].<ref name="Slotnik-2019"/> He quit shortly after training camp started and played a season with the [[Chicago Owls]] in the [[Continental Football League]].<ref name="Notre Dame Fighting Irish - Official Athletics Website-2019" /> Kuechenberg signed with the Dolphins as a [[free agent]] in [[1970 NFL season|1970]].<ref name="Slotnik-2019"/> He became a starter that season, starting 5 out of 14 games played,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bob Kuechenberg Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/K/KuecBo00.htm |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> as the Dolphins finished 10–4 and made the playoffs for the first time in club history. During the next regular season, 1971, Kuechenberg helped the Dolphins make it to the Super Bowl, where they lost to the [[1971 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]] 24–3.<ref name="Pro-Football-Reference.com">{{Cite web |title=Miami Dolphins Team Records, Leaders, and League Ranks |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/mia/index.htm |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl VI - Dallas Cowboys vs. Miami Dolphins - January 16th, 1972 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197201160dal.htm |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

The next two seasons the Dolphins won the Super Bowl (going 17–0 in 1972)<ref name="Pro-Football-Reference.com" /> and his play was noticed by New York Post writer [[Paul Zimmerman (sportswriter)|Paul Zimmerman]], who named Kuechenberg on his All-pro ballot.{{citation needed|date=November 2024}} The following season, 1974, he was named All-AFC by Pro Football Weekly and was named to his first Pro Bowl. In total, he would play in six Pro Bowls 1974–1975, 1977–1978, 1982–1983. He was named 1st team All-Pro in [[1975 NFL season|1975]] and in [[1978 NFL season|1978]] and was named All-[[American Football Conference|AFC]] three times. He was Second-team All-Pro in 1977. He played in four Super Bowls (in 1971, 1972, 1973, and 1982), winning in 1972 and 1973. He was a team captain from 1980 to 1984. In 1995, he was inducted into the [[Miami Dolphins Honor Roll]]. His 19 playoff games are the most in Dolphins' history.<ref name="Indiana Football Hall of Fame" /><ref name="Notre Dame Fighting Irish - Official Athletics Website-2019" />

Kuechenberg was sometimes critical of his past teams.  One such critique prompted then-current Miami All-Pro, [[Jason Taylor (American football)|Jason Taylor]], to comment, "It's another chapter in the grumpy Kuechenberg story. It's Kuechenberg. He gets up every year and complains about something. If it ain't one thing, it's another. He needs a hug and a hobby. It's ridiculous."<ref>{{cite news |author=Maske, Mark |title=J. Taylor Sticks Up For Beleaguered Dolphins |url=http://blog.washingtonpost.com/nflinsider/2006/11/j_taylor_sticks_up_for_beleagu.html |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=November 2, 2006 |access-date=2010-03-08 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110523090215/http://blog.washingtonpost.com/nflinsider/2006/11/j_taylor_sticks_up_for_beleagu.html |archive-date=May 23, 2011 }}</ref>

Kuechenberg was inducted into the American Football Association's Semi Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1986.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.americanfootballassn.com/forms/2010HallofFameListing.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2011-08-28 |archive-date=2016-01-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160122083011/http://www.americanfootballassn.com/forms/2010HallofFameListing.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] honored the entire 1972 Perfect Season Dolphins at an event in the [[White House]], but Kuechenberg declined to attend for political reasons.<ref name= "Hamnik"/><ref name=MH081913>{{cite web|first=Greg|last=Cote|url=http://www.miamiherald.com/2013/08/19/v-fullstory/3573584/greg-cote-white-house-invite-a.html|title=White House invite a last stamp of approval for '72 Miami Dolphins|date=20 August 2013|work=[[The Miami Herald|MiamiHerald.com]]|publisher=Miami Herald Media|access-date=20 August 2013| archive-date=20 August 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130820035855/http://www.miamiherald.com/2013/08/19/v-fullstory/3573584/greg-cote-white-house-invite-a.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Darlington |first=Jim |title=President Obama honors 1972 Miami Dolphins at White House |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/president-obama-honors-1972-miami-dolphins-at-white-house-0ap1000000232205 |date=20 August 2013 |work=[[National Football League|NFL.com]] |publisher=NFL Enterprises |access-date=20 August 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130821213603/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap1000000232205/article/president-obama-honors-1972-miami-dolphins-at-white-house |archive-date=21 August 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Brian |last=McIntyre |title=Three members of the 1972 Miami Dolphins to skip White House visit for political reasons |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/blogs/nfl-shutdown-corner/three-members-1972-miami-dolphins-skip-white-house-154517369.html?.tsrc=attmp |work=[[Yahoo! Sports|Sports.yahoo.com]] |series=Shutdown Corner |publisher=[[Yahoo!]] |date=20 August 2013 |access-date=20 August 2013 |archive-date=16 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131216203726/http://sports.yahoo.com/blogs/nfl-shutdown-corner/three-members-1972-miami-dolphins-skip-white-house-154517369.html?.tsrc=attmp |url-status=dead }}</ref>  He told sports columnist [[Dave Hyde]] of [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida|Ft. Lauderdale's]] ''[[Sun Sentinel|Sun-Sentinel]]'' "I want to be careful, because Mom said if you have nothing good to say about someone, then don't say anything. I don't have anything good to say about someone."<ref>{{cite web|last=Hyde|first=Dave|title=At least three '72 Dolphins refuse White House invite|url=http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/2013-08-17/sports/fl-dave-hyde-white-house-dolphins-0818-20130817_1_white-house-president-obama-bob-kuechenberg|work=[[Sun-Sentinel|Sun-Sentinel.com]]|publisher=Howard Greenberg ([[Tribune Company]])|access-date=20 August 2013|author-link=Dave Hyde|date=17 August 2013|archive-date=21 August 2013|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130821030836/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/2013-08-17/sports/fl-dave-hyde-white-house-dolphins-0818-20130817_1_white-house-president-obama-bob-kuechenberg|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2014, he was inducted into the [[Chicagoland Sports Hall of Fame]], and was given its George Connor Lifetime Achievement Award.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-09-16 |title=Kuechenberg, Zbikowski Join Chicagoland Sports Hall of Fame |url=https://fightingirish.com/kuechenberg-zbikowski-join-chicagoland-sports-hall-of-fame/ |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=Notre Dame Fighting Irish - Official Athletics Website |language=en-US}}</ref> The [[Professional Football Researchers Association]] named Kuechenberg to the PRFA Hall of Very Good Class of 2013.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.profootballresearchers.com/hall-of-very-good-2013.htm |title=Professional Researchers Association Hall of Very Good Class of 2013 |access-date=November 10, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170104015529/http://www.profootballresearchers.com/hall-of-very-good-2013.htm |archive-date=January 4, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was a finalist on a number of occasions for the Hall of Fame, but has not made it.<ref name="Slotnik-2019"/> As of October 22, 2024, he remained a candidate in the seniors category for inclusion in the hall of fame class for 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=31 Seniors remain in consideration for Pro Football Hall of Fame's Class of 2025 {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2024/10/31-seniors-remain-in-consideration-for-hall%E2%80%99s-class-of-2025-after-second-reduction-vote/ |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> He did not make the final round.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Contributor, coach, senior finalists revealed for Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2025 |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/contributor-coach-senior-finalists-revealed-for-pro-football-hall-of-fame-class-of-2025#:~:text=The%2025%20players%20still%20under,Jahri%20Evans,%20Richmond%20Webb,%20Steve |access-date=2024-12-06 |website=NFL.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Health and death ==
Kuechenberg played with various significant injuries. He played Super Bowl VIII with a fractured arm. He completed a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers, even though he had suffered a broken ankle. He played much of 1977 with two bone fractures in his back. His career ended after an eye injury in 1983.<ref name="Slotnik-2019"/> Legendary ''[[The New York Times|New York Times]]'' sportswriter [[Red Smith (sportswriter)|Red Smith]] quoted Kuechenberg in 1975, on his sacrifice and strategy for success against opposing defensive tackles: "'I just fight him .... As long as he's beating on my head and not the quarterback's it's all right with me.'"<ref name="Slotnik-2019"/>

He was one of at least 345 [[List of NFL players with chronic traumatic encephalopathy|NFL players to be diagnosed after death with chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] (CTE), which is caused by repeated hits to the head.<ref>{{cite news |title=The driving force behind Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) |url=https://concussionfoundation.org/cte-resources/subconcussive-impacts |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230702123543/https://concussionfoundation.org/cte-resources/subconcussive-impacts |archive-date=July 2, 2023 |access-date=July 2, 2023 |website=Concussion Legacy Foundation}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Ken Belson and Benjamin Mueller |date=June 20, 2023 |title=Collective Force of Head Hits, Not Just the Number of Them, Increases Odds of C.T.E. The largest study of chronic traumatic encephalopathy to date found that the cumulative force of head hits absorbed by players in their careers is the best predictor of future brain disease. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/20/sports/football/cte-study-concussions-brain-tackle.html |access-date=July 2, 2023 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> He was diagnosed posthumously, and among six Dolphins from the 1972 team diagnosed with CTE (Kuechenberg, [[Jim Kiick]], [[Jake Scott]], [[Bill Stanfill]], [[Earl Morrall]] and [[Nick Buoniconti]]).<ref>{{Cite news |last=Belson |first=Ken |date=February 12, 2022 |title=For N.F.L. Perfection, a Steep Price |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/12/sports/football/dolphins-nfl-cte.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> More recently, another 15 Dolphins have been discovered to have had CTE.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Habib |first=Hal |title=Twenty-one former Dolphins had CTE, Boston University research study reveals |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/sports/nfl/2023/02/07/cte-found-in-21-former-dolphins-boston-university-research-reveals/69881861007/ |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=The Palm Beach Post |language=en-US}}</ref> Kuechenberg likely had thousands of head hits during the years he played football. After his death and CTE diagnosis, researchers asked his daughter if the family knew how many concussions Kuechenberg suffered. She told them "'His head was his tool. ... Do that math over college and high school.'" She stated that her father declined rapidly in the years leading to his death, his memory beginning to fail, rarely leaving home, making poor financial decisions, drinking heavily, suffering from depression and contemplating suicide.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2020-02-02 |title=The perfect '72 Miami Dolphins and football's ultimate toll (from the New York Times) |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2020/02/02/the-perfect-72-miami-dolphins-and-footballs-ultimate-toll/ |access-date=2024-11-17 |website=Chicago Tribune |language=en-US}}</ref>

He died of a heart attack on January 12, 2019.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Neal |first=David J. |date=January 13, 2019 |title=Dolphins' Super Bowl-era All-Pro guard Bob Kuechenberg dies at 71 |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/sports/nfl/miami-dolphins/article224478905.html |work=Miami Herald}}</ref>

'''Robert Ross Lurtsema''' (born March 29, 1942) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] for the [[Minnesota Vikings]], [[New York Giants]] and [[Seattle Seahawks]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Western Michigan Broncos football|Western Michigan Broncos]]. Lurtsema played in two [[Super Bowl]]s with the Vikings.

Born in [[Grand Rapids, Michigan]], Lurtsema attended Ottawa Hills High School and initially went to [[Michigan Technological University|Michigan Tech]] in 1962 on a basketball scholarship, but started playing football and lettered in the sport as a Huskie in  the 1962 season.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mlive.com/sports/g66l-2019/11/913a74b6b73621/25-greatest-football-players-of-all-time-from-the-grand-rapids-area.html|title=25 greatest football players of all time from the Grand Rapids area|date=November 13, 2019|website=mlive}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.michigantechhuskies.com/sports/fball/archives/letterwinners|title=All-Time Michigan Tech Football Letterwinners|website=Michigan Tech Athletics}}</ref> Lurtsema transferred to [[Western Michigan University]] to continue his collegiate career, lettering in football as a Bronco in 1965.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wmubroncos.com/documents/2020/7/24/2020_Guide.pdf|title=2020 Football Media Guide Guide (PDF)|website=Western Michigan University Athletics}}</ref> Undrafted after graduating, Lurtsema played for the 1966 Harrisburg Capitals of the [[Atlantic Coast Football League]], which was a taxi squad affiliated with the [[Baltimore Colts]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/1966acflharr.html|title=1966 Harrisburg Capitols - Pro Football Archives|website=www.profootballarchives.com}}</ref> [[Don Shula]], Colts coach, had drafted [[Bubba Smith]] in 1967, blocking an opportunity for Lurtsema. Shula arranged a trade to the [[New York Giants]]. Lurtsema said of Shula, "I owe everything to Shula. He basically set up my whole career.  I can’t say enough good things about him.”<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.startribune.com/former-vikings-defensive-lineman-bob-lurtsema-says-he-owes-his-career-to-don-shula/570193832/|title=Former Vikings defensive lineman Bob Lurtsema says he owes his career to Don Shula|website=Star Tribune}}</ref>

Lurtsema played with the [[New York Giants]] for 1967, making the all-rookie team in 1967 and the [[The Sporting News|Sporting News]] All-Star team in 1968.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1968/allpro.htm|title=1968 NFL All-Pros|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref> He became a regular starter for the Giants through the 1971 season, changing positions in 1970 from defensive tackle to defensive end, but the Giants waived him at the end of the 1971 season.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1971/11/11/archives/an-embittered-lurtsema-is-dropped-by-the-giants-bitter-lurtsema-let.html|title=An Embittered Lurtsema Is Dropped by the Giants (Published 1971)|first=Al|last=Harvin|work=The New York Times |date=November 11, 1971|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref>

The [[Minnesota Vikings]] signed Lurtsema in 1972. In the third game of the [[Miami Dolphins]] 1972 NFL season, the Dolphins appeared to be on the way to losing a game against the Vikings. Lurtsema was flagged for roughing the passer in a pivotal play in the game, and for the Dolphins' season, as they ended up undefeated.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.startribune.com/bob-lurtsema-s-penalty-the-play-that-changed-the-course-of-the-1972-season/492262251/|title=Bob Lurtsema's penalty: the play that changed the course of the 1972 season|website=Star Tribune}}</ref> Lurtsema played regularly for the Vikings and back up the famed [[Purple People Eaters]] defensive line, but he rarely started, earning the affectionate nickname "Benchwarmer Bob."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1973/12/23/archives/the-purple-people-eaters-a-team-within-a-team-within-a-team.html|title=A team within a team within a team (Published 1973)|first=Peter Ross|last=Range|work=The New York Times |date=December 23, 1973|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref> Lurtsema played for the Vikings in [[Super Bowl VIII]] in 1974 and [[Super Bowl IX]] in 1975, both losing causes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197401130mia.htm|title=Super Bowl VIII - Minnesota Vikings vs. Miami Dolphins - January 13th, 1974|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/photos/super-bowl-viii-09000d5d803c09fa|title=Super Bowl VIII|website=NFL.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197501120min.htm|title=Super Bowl IX - Pittsburgh Steelers vs. Minnesota Vikings - January 12th, 1975|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/photos/super-bowl-ix-09000d5d803c0e37|title=Super Bowl IX|website=NFL.com}}</ref>

The Vikings traded Lurtsema to the [[Seattle Seahawks]], an expansion team in their first season in 1976 in a deal for wide receiver [[Ahmad Rashad]]. Lurtsema played two seasons in Seattle, starting regularly at defensive end.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LurtBo20.htm|title=Bob Lurtsema Stats|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref> He retired after the 1977 NFL season with 82 career starts.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vikings.com/news/bob-lurtsema-day-throwback|title=Throwback: 'Bob Lurtsema Day'|website=www.vikings.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vikings.com/news/benchwarmer-bob-trade-started-vikings-seahawks-exchange-16669031|title='Benchwarmer Bob' Trade Started Vikings-Seahawks Exchange|website=www.vikings.com}}</ref>

After retirement, Lurtsema often appeared as "Benchwarmer Bob" in television commercials for [[TCF Financial Corporation]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.twincities.com/2010/12/14/charley-walters-bob-lurtsema-warms-the-bench-for-his-50-greatest-vikings/|title=Charley Walters: Bob Lurtsema warms the bench for his 50 greatest Vikings|date=December 14, 2010}}</ref>

Lurtsema pitched for the [[Minnesota Norsemen]] professional softball team during their 1979 season in the [[Men's professional softball in the United States|American Professional Slo-Pitch League (APSPL)]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8562140/twins-debut-st-story/|title=Twins debut ST story|newspaper=Star Tribune |date=July 22, 1979|pages=34|via=newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/64705361/the-minneapolis-star/|title=Clipped From The Minneapolis Star|newspaper=The Minneapolis Star |date=May 18, 1979|pages=51|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>  He also owned Benchwarmer Bob's Sports Cafe, which had two locations in the [[Twin Cities]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.twincities.com/2007/02/13/burnsville-popular-sports-bar-closes/|title=Burnsville / Popular sports bar closes|date=February 13, 2007}}</ref>

In 1990, Lurtsema wrestled a match for [[American Wrestling Association]]'s AWA Twin Wars teaming with [[Brad Rheingans]] and [[Patriot (wrestler)|The Trooper]] defeating [[Tully Blanchard]] and the [[Beverly Brothers|Destruction Crew]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.profightdb.com/wrestlers/bob-lurtsema-19557.html |title=Bob Lurtsema: Profile & Match Listing - Internet Wrestling Database (IWD) }}</ref>

In 2013, Lurtsema signed on to support the lawsuit brought against the NFL in regard to [[concussions in American football|concussions in the sport]]. He advocated for the funds to be used for players impacted by injuries and for research into brain injuries.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/blog/minnesota-vikings/post/_/id/159/lurtsema-spend-lawsuit-money-wisely|title=Lurtsema: Spend lawsuit money wisely|date=August 30, 2013|website=ESPN.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://columbiasportsjournalism.com/2014/02/02/the-funny-mans-serious-side/|title=| The Funny Man's Serious SideColumbia Sports Journalism}}</ref> Lurtsema and his wife Aloise are retired and live in [[Minnesota]].

[[Weber State Wildcats football|Weber State]] (1967–1970) | draftyear = 1971 | draftround = 11 | draftpick = 262 | pastteams = * [[New Orleans Saints]] ({{NFL Year|1971|1977}}) * [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] ({{NFL Year|1978|1981}}) | highlights = * [[New Orleans Saints Hall of Fame]] | statlabel1 = [[Quarterback sack|Sacks]] | statvalue1 = 57 | statlabel2 = [[Fumble]] recoveries | statvalue2 = 14 | statlabel3 = Defensive [[touchdown]]s | statvalue3 = 1 | pfr = P/PollBo20 }} '''Robert Lee Pollard''' (born December 30, 1948) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for 11 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[New Orleans Saints]]—where he played four seasons as a [[defensive tackle]]—and the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Southern Tigers football|Texas Southern Tigers]] and the [[Weber State Wildcats football|Weber State Wildcats]] and was selected by the Saints in the eleventh round of the [[1971 NFL draft]]. ==Early life== Pollard attended the black [[Hebert High School]] in [[Beaumont, Texas]]. ==College career== He began his [[college football]] career in 1966 with the [[Texas Southern Tigers football|Texas Southern Tigers]], as he wanted to stay close to his family. After a year and a half, he decided to transfer to the [[Weber State Wildcats football|Weber State Wildcats]] even though he had been a starter at Texas Southern because he felt that the school was trying to take his scholarship away in order to offer it to talented out of state players.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m5uzDwAAQBAJ&dq=bob+pollard+texas+southern+football&pg=PT259|title = Black Man in the Huddle: Stories from the Integration of Texas Football|isbn = 9781623497521|last1 = Jacobus|first1 = Robert D.|date = October 3, 2019| publisher=Texas A&M University Press }} ==Professional career== He was selected by the [[New Orleans Saints]] with the 262nd overall pick of the [[1971 NFL draft]]. Although [[quarterback sack]]s were not officially recorded prior to 1982, he has been credited with 57 unofficial sacks during his career.{{cite web |last=Lynch |first=Mike |date=July 12, 2021 |title=Pre-1982 Sacks Added To Pro Football Reference |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/blog/2021/07/pre-1982-sacks-added-to-pro-football-reference/ |access-date=April 11, 2026 |website=Sports Reference}} ==After football== In 1971, Pollard was one of sixteen pro football players from Beaumont to be given the [[Freedom of the city|Keys to The City]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.dallasnews.com/high-school-sports/2017/07/22/flashback-dfw-produces-a-ton-of-football-talent-but-another-part-of-texas-is-the-pro-football-capital-of-the-world/|title = Flashback: DFW produces a ton of football talent, but another part of Texas is 'the pro football capital of the world'|date = July 22, 2017}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.brown.edu/Departments/Joukowsky_Institute/courses/13things/7443.html#:~:text=This%20medieval%20tradition%20is%20meant,trusted%20friend%20of%20city%20residents.|title=Key to the City}} ==Personal life== His son, [[Robert Pollard (American football)|Robert]], had a brief NFL career as a defensive end with the [[San Diego Chargers]] and the [[Seattle Seahawks]].{{cite web|title=Robert Pollard|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/PollRo20.htm|publisher=Sports Reference|work=Pro Football Reference|accessdate=2023-05-11}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Saints1971DraftPicks}} {{New Orleans Saints Hall of Fame}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Pollard, Bob}} [[Category:1948 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:Players of American football from Beaumont, Texas]] [[Category:American football defensive ends]] [[Category:American football defensive tackles]] [[Category:Weber State Wildcats football players]] [[Category:New Orleans Saints players]] [[Category:St. Louis Cardinals (football) players]] [[Category:20th-century American sportsmen]]

'''Robert Charles Swenson''' (born July 1, 1953) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for the [[Denver Broncos]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[California Golden Bears football|California Golden Bears]]. He joined the NFL in 1975 as an [[undrafted free agent]] and played the Broncos.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Bob Swenson |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SwenBo00.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220924163100/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SwenBo00.htm |archive-date=2022-09-24 |access-date=2023-05-11 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Commenting on the draft for ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' in 1978, Swenson said that "The draft is bull,... The scouts for most of the teams are 100 years old, and most of them don't know what they're doing. I went to school at Berkeley, and most of the NFL scouts think the students are still rioting in the streets out there. They didn't want to look at me."<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Jenkins |first=Dan |date=1978-01-23 |title=Doomsday in the Dome |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/features/superbowl/archives/12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130207042516/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/features/superbowl/archives/12 |archive-date=2013-02-07 |magazine=Sports Illustrated}}</ref>

Swenson's career spanned eight seasons, from 1975 through 1983, though he missed the 1980 season due to an injury.<ref name=":0" /> He was part of the famed [[Orange Crush Defense]] that propelled the Broncos to [[Super Bowl XII]] in January 1978, at the end of the 1977 season.{{Citation needed|date=May 2023}} He was elected to the [[Pro Bowl]] after the [[1981 NFL season|1981 season]].<ref name=":0" />

Linebackers/special teams coach * [[Minnesota Golden Gophers football|Minnesota]] (1988–1991)
Assistant coach | highlights = * 2× [[List of Super Bowl champions|Super Bowl champion]] ([[Super Bowl VII|VII]], [[Super Bowl VIII|VIII]]) * First-team [[All-America college football team|All-American]] ([[1966 All-America college football team|1966]]) * 2× First-team [[List of All-Atlantic Coast Conference football teams|All-ACC]] ([[1965 All-Atlantic Coast Conference football team|1965]], [[1966 All-Atlantic Coast Conference football team|1966]]) | statlabel1 = [[Interception]]s | statvalue1 = 12 | statlabel2 = [[Fumble]] recoveries | statvalue2 = 10 | statlabel3 = [[Quarterback sack|Sack]]s | statvalue3 = 15.0 | pfr = MathBo20 }} '''Robert Matheson''' (November 25, 1944 – September 5, 1994) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[linebacker]] who played 13 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played in three [[Super Bowls]] for the [[Miami Dolphins]], including their 1972 and 1973 championships. A linebacker at [[Duke University]], he was drafted in 1967 by the [[Cleveland Brown]]s in the first round of the NFL Draft, which was the first year of the common draft between the AFL and NFL. He was then acquired by the Dolphins prior to the 1971 season, after Miami defensive coordinator [[Bill Arnsparger]] requested head coach [[Don Shula]] to do so. Miami gave up their second round draft pick in 1972 in exchange.{{cite news |title=Matheson Swells Linebacking Corp |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/24431489/the-miami-news/ |newspaper=[[The Miami News]] |location=[[Miami|Miami, Florida]] |date=September 2, 1971 |page=20 |access-date=October 10, 2018 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] {{Open access}} }} Matheson went to Miami one year after the Dolphins acquired [[Paul Warfield]] from Cleveland. Matheson's versatility against both the run and pass was at the heart of the "53" defense, a scheme that was named for his jersey number and devised by Arnsparger. Depending on whether the situation was running or passing, he was a strong-side defensive end and a fourth linebacker respectively.[https://www.nytimes.com/1974/01/13/archives/matheson-is-key-to-miami-53-defense-follow-dotted-line.html "Matheson Is Key to Miami '53 Defense,'" ''The New York Times'', Sunday 13 January 1974.] Retrieved 15 September 2025. The latter is also referred to as a [[3–4 defense]], with three linemen and four linebackers.[https://www.miamiherald.com/sports/nfl/miami-dolphins/article27521356.html Neal, David J. "Former Miami Dolphins defensive icon Bill Arnsparger dies at 88," ''Miami Herald'', Friday 17 July 2015.] Retrieved 15 September 2025.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}} After leaving the Dolphins in 1979, Matheson returned to Duke as an assistant coach. He later coached special teams and linebackers for five years with the Miami Dolphins. He then joined Duke alumni [[John Gutekunst]] as an assistant coach at the [[University of Minnesota]]. In 1993, he returned to Duke to work at its Comprehensive Cancer Center. Matheson died on September 5, 1994, at [[Duke University Health System|Duke University Hospital]] from complications of [[Hodgkin lymphoma|Hodgkin's disease]], which he had had for 13 years.{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/09/07/obituaries/bob-matheson-football-player-49.html | title=Bob Matheson; Football Player, 49 | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] | date=September 7, 1994 | access-date=November 9, 2007}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Navboxes|title=|list= {{1967 NFL Draft}} {{Browns1967DraftPicks}} {{BrownsFirstPick}} {{Super Bowl VII}} {{Super Bowl VIII}} }} {{DEFAULTSORT:Matheson, Bob}} [[Category:1944 births]] [[Category:1994 deaths]] [[Category:American football linebackers]] [[Category:Cleveland Browns players]] [[Category:Duke Blue Devils football coaches]] [[Category:Duke Blue Devils football players]] [[Category:Miami Dolphins coaches]] [[Category:Miami Dolphins players]] [[Category:Minnesota Golden Gophers football coaches]] [[Category:People from Boone, North Carolina]] [[Category:Coaches of American football from North Carolina]] [[Category:Players of American football from North Carolina]] [[Category:Deaths from Hodgkin lymphoma]] [[Category:Deaths from lymphoma in North Carolina]] [[Category:20th-century American sportsmen]] {{linebacker-1940s-stub}}

([[Pen Argyl, Pennsylvania]]) | college = [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State]] | draftyear = 1972 | draftround = 5 | draftpick = 117 | pastteams = * [[Chicago Bears]] ({{NFL Year|1972|1983}}) * [[Birmingham Stallions]] ({{USFL Year|1984}}–{{USFL Year|1985}}) | highlights = * 2× [[List of National Football League annual punting yards leaders|NFL punting yards leader]] (1981, 1982) * First-team All-East ([[1971 All-East football team|1971]]) ; NFL record * Most punts in a season: 114 (1981){{efn|Tied with [[Chad Stanley]]}} | statlabel1 = [[Punt (gridiron football)|Punts]] | statvalue1 = 884 | statlabel2 = [[Punt (gridiron football)|Punt yards]] | statvalue2 = 34,180 | statlabel3 = Punting average | statvalue3 = 38.7 | statlabel4 = [[Punt (gridiron football)|Longest punt]] | statvalue4 = 81 | statlabel5 = Inside 20 | statvalue5 = 157 | statlabel6 = [[Reception (gridiron football)|Receptions]] | statvalue6 = 19 | statlabel7 = [[Reception (gridiron football)|Receiving yards]] | statvalue7 = 231 | statlabel8 = [[Touchdown|Receiving TDs]] | statvalue8 = 4 | pfr = P/ParsBo00 }} '''Robert Herber Parsons''' (June 29, 1950 – July 8, 2022) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[punter (gridiron football)|punter]] and [[tight end]] who played twelve seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played for the [[Chicago Bears]] from 1972 to 1983 and later played with the [[Birmingham Stallions]] of the [[United States Football League]] (USFL). He holds the NFL record for most punts in a season with 114, set in 1981; [[Chad Stanley]] tied the record in 2002.{{Cite web|url=https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2022/07/13/nfl-single-season-punt-leader-bob-parsons-dies-at-72/|title=NFL single-season punt leader Bob Parsons dies at 72|date=July 13, 2022|work=Pro Football Talk}} ==Early life== Parsons was born in [[Bethlehem, Pennsylvania]], on June 29, 1950. He attended [[Pen Argyl Area High School]] in nearby [[Pen Argyl, Pennsylvania|Pen Argyl]].{{cite web|title=Bob Parsons Stats|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/ParsBo00.htm|access-date=July 13, 2022|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC}} He then studied at [[Pennsylvania State University]].{{cite news|title=Former Penn State tight end, long-time Chicago Bear dies|url=https://www.pennlive.com/pennstatefootball/2022/07/former-penn-state-tight-end-long-time-chicago-bear-has-passed-away.html|first=Brian|last=Linder|date=July 13, 2022|access-date=July 13, 2022|newspaper=The Patriot-News|location=Harrisburg, Pennsylvania|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220713131000/https://www.pennlive.com/pennstatefootball/2022/07/former-penn-state-tight-end-long-time-chicago-bear-has-passed-away.html|archivedate=July 13, 2022|url-status=live}} ==College career== Parsons played for the [[Penn State Nittany Lions]], which was coached by [[Joe Paterno]] at the time. He saw his first game action during the 1969 season as the team's third-string quarterback. Playing behind starter [[Chuck Burkhart]] and Mike Cooper, Parsons saw limited action, appearing in a couple of games, complete five of twelve passes and one interception. Penn State finished second in the AP poll that year. With Burkhart graduated, Parsons moved up to second string behind Cooper on a stacked squad that featured future NFL stars [[Franco Harris]] and [[Lydell Mitchell]] in the backfield. With the veteran Burkhart gone, and only Cooper and Parsons at the helm, Penn State slipped to 7–3 in 1970. The following season, Paterno made a radical change to the quarterback position. He named [[John Hufnagel]] as the starter and made Parsons a tight end. In his first and only college season as a receiver, Parsons responded by catching 30 passes for 489 yards and 5 touchdown receptions.{{Cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/bob-parsons-1.html|title=Bob Parsons College Stats}} Penn State took on Texas at the conclusion of the season in the Cotton Bowl. The Nittany Lions routed the Longhorns, 30–6, A key 19 yard pass from Hufnagel to Parsons helped set up a Penn state score.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1972/01/02/archives/lions-rout-texas-on-2dhalf-surge-penn-state-306-victor-in-cotton.html|title = LIONS ROUT TEXAS ON 2D-HALF SURGE Penn State 30-6 Victor in Cotton Bowl—Recovery of Fumbles Spurs Drive|newspaper = The New York Times|date = 2 January 1972}} ==Professional career== Parsons was drafted by the [[Chicago Bears]] in the fifth round (117th overall selection) of the [[1972 NFL draft]]. He made the team as a rookie, playing behind starter Earl Thomas. The Bears finished 4–9–1 under head coach [[Abe Gibron]],{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/chi/1972.htm|title=1972 Chicago Bears Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees, Injury Reports|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=July 13, 2022}} but Parsons scored a touchdown during rookie season, in his first game as a pro.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/ParsBo00/gamelog/1972/|title=Bob Parsons 1972 Game Log|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=July 13, 2022}} Not long after [[Atlanta Falcons]] defensive end [[John Zook]] returned a fumble for a score, Bears quarterback Bobby Douglas found Parsons for a game tying six yard touchdown pass. That would be as close as the Bears would get, as the Falcons routed Chicago 37–21.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197209170chi.htm|title = Atlanta Falcons at Chicago Bears – September 17th, 1972 |work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC }} Parsons remained a back-up tight end the following season, catching a few passes throughout the season. The Bears fell to 3–11 in 1973 under Gibron.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/chi/1973.htm|title=1973 Chicago Bears Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees, Injury Reports|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=July 13, 2022}} Parsons became a starter for the first time in his pro career the following year, changing positions from tight end to punter in order to replace [[Bobby Joe Green]].{{cite news|title=Former Bears punter and tight end dies at age 72|url=https://www.si.com/nfl/bears/news/bob-parsons-made-884-punts-from-1975-83|first=Gene|last=Chamberlain|date=July 13, 2022|accessdate=July 13, 2022|work=SI.com|publisher=Sports Illustrated}} In his first season as a punter, Parsons punted 90 times for a 37.9 yard average with one punt blocked. However, the Bears once again finished the season with double digit losses.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/chi/1974.htm|title=1974 Chicago Bears Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees, Injury Reports|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=July 13, 2022}} The 1975 season saw the arrival of new head coach [[Jack Pardee]] and rookie running back [[Walter Payton]]. Parsons was even doing double duty. He was the team's punter as well as the starting tight end. That season Parsons caught 13 passes for 184 yards, and a touchdown, his first since the first game of his rookie season. Parsons' second career touchdown came from quarterback Gary Huff in the Bears 27–14 win over the rival [[Green Bay Packers]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197511090chi.htm|title = Green Bay Packers at Chicago Bears – November 9th, 1975 |work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC}} In 1976, Parsons was back to being the team's punter, though he did complete two passes during the season. One was a 23-yard pass against the [[Detroit Lions]] week one, and the second one a 25-yard pass week eight against the [[Minnesota Vikings]]. Both games were Bears victories.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/ParsBo00/gamelog/1976/|title=Bob Parsons 1976 Game Log|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=July 13, 2022}} In 1977, the Bears finally had a winning season, going 9–5, and making the playoffs.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/chi/1977.htm|title=1977 Chicago Bears Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees, Injury Reports|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=July 13, 2022}} However, they lost to the [[Dallas Cowboys]] 37–7, with Parsons punting six times that game as the Bears offense struggled to get on track.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197712260dal.htm|title=Divisional Round – Chicago Bears at Dallas Cowboys – December 26th, 1977|date=December 26, 1977|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=July 13, 2022}} After the conclusion of the 1977 season, Pardee left to coach the [[Washington Redskins]] and Neill Armstrong succeeded him as the Bears head coach. While the Bears slipped to 7–9, Parsons had himself as the Bears punter.{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/chi/1978.htm|title=1978 Chicago Bears Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees, Injury Reports|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=July 13, 2022}} He would remain so until 1983, when [[Mike Ditka]] cut Parsons after week 14 and replaced him with ex-Packers punter [[Ray Stachowicz]]. Ditka had become enraged when he learned that Parsons had been talking to the owners of the [[Chicago Blitz]] of the USFL about signing on as the team's punter of the possibility of a role as a special teams coach. Ditka, already reeling from quarterback [[Vince Evans]] pending departure to the upstart spring league, and that the league had been talking to other members of the Bears, cut Parsons, citing he only wanted players that would be loyal to the Bears.{{Cite web|first1=Randy|last1=Minkoff|date=5 December 1983|work=UPI|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1983/12/05/An-angry-Chicago-Bears-Coach-Mike-Ditka-said-Monday/4650439448400/|title = An angry Chicago Bears Coach Mike Ditka said Monday}} After departing the Bears, Parsons signed with the [[Birmingham Stallions]] of the USFL. The team managed to sign quarterback [[Cliff Stoudt]] away from the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]],{{cite news|title=A time for the Stoudt of heart|url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1984/03/19/a-time-for-the-stoudt-of-heart|first=Franz|last=Lidz|date=March 19, 1984|accessdate=July 13, 2022|work=SI.com|publisher=Sports Illustrated}} and running back [[Joe Cribbs]] from the Buffalo Bills.{{cite news|title=Birmingham Stallions running back Joe Cribbs, who was obtained…|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1984/05/09/Birmingham-Stallions-running-back-Joe-Cribbs-who-was-obtained/2152452923200/|first=Harold|last=Jackson|date=May 9, 1984|access-date=July 13, 2022|work=United Press International}} In a 1985 playoff game against the [[Houston Gamblers]], led by quarterback Jim Kelly, the Stallions eliminated Houston, thanks in part to Parsons punt that pinned Houston on their own one yard line.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/06/30/sports/stallions-eliminate-gamblers.html|title=Stallions Eliminate Gamblers|newspaper=The New York Times|date=30 June 1985}} During his time the Stallions, Parsons served mainly as the team's punter. In 1984, he punted 42 times for 1,625 yards. In 1985, he punted 67 times for 2,626 yards.{{cite web| url = https://www.justsportsstats.com/footballstatsindex.php?player_id=parsobob001| title = Robert Parsons football statistics on StatsCrew.com}} After the 1985 season, with the USFL's future in doubt due to a lawsuit against the NFL, Parsons retired from pro football.{{cite news|title=Former Bears punter died last Friday, team says|url=https://www.nbcsports.com/chicago/bears/former-chicago-bears-punter-bob-parsons-died-last-friday-team-says|first=Ryan|last=Taylor|date=July 13, 2022|access-date=July 13, 2022|publisher=NBC News}} During the 1975, 1981 and 1982 seasons, Parsons led the NFL in punting attempts, while leading the NFL in punt yards in both 1982 and 1983. '''Robert Kowalkowski''' (November 5, 1943 – September 17, 2009) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[Guard (gridiron football)|offensive guard]] who played for the [[Detroit Lions]] and the [[Green Bay Packers]] in a twelve-year career that lasted from 1966 to 1977 in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).<ref>{{cite web|title=Former Lions Lineman Bob Kowalkowski Dies|url=http://www.detroitlions.com/news/article-1/Former-Lions-Lineman-Bob-Kowalkowski-Dies/2eb89c42-db31-4a90-a7c1-08da9c3ea846|website=Detroitlions.com|accessdate=25 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180326063922/http://www.detroitlions.com/news/article-1/Former-Lions-Lineman-Bob-Kowalkowski-Dies/2eb89c42-db31-4a90-a7c1-08da9c3ea846|archive-date=26 March 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Kowalkowski played college football at the [[University of Virginia]] and was drafted in the fifth round of the [[1965 NFL draft]] by the Lions.  His son [[Scott Kowalkowski|Scott]] was selected in the [[1991 NFL draft]] by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] and also played with the Lions.<ref>{{cite web|title=Longtime Lions lineman Kowalkowski dies at 65|url=http://www.espn.co.uk/nfl/news/story?id=4484301|website=ESPN.com|accessdate=25 March 2018|date=18 September 2009}}</ref>

'''Robert Lee Newton''' (born August 16, 1949) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[guard (American football)|guard]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1971 to 1981.

==Early life==
Newton was voted most improved player his junior year and "most valuable lineman" and All-League defensive tackle his senior year at [[John Glenn High School (California)|John Glenn High School]].<ref name="BlogTalkRadio tutor">{{Cite web |url=http://www.blogtalkradio.com/totaltutor/2015/05/15/nfl-star-and-nebraska-football-star-bob-newton |title=NFL Star and Nebraska Football Star Bob Newton 05/14 by Total Tutor | Education Podcasts |access-date=2015-05-21 |archive-date=2015-09-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924003234/http://www.blogtalkradio.com/totaltutor/2015/05/15/nfl-star-and-nebraska-football-star-bob-newton |url-status=dead }}</ref> He then played for two seasons (1967–68) at [[Cerritos College]] and won named 2nd Team All-Conference and earned the team's Most Outstanding Offensive Lineman.

== College career ==
At Nebraska

Coach Bob Devaney labeled Newton as a lineman “who definitely should be considered as an All-American” and Bob delivered in 1970. Newton stepped in as a transfer star in 1969 and earned consensus All-America and unanimous All-Big Eight honors in 1970. Set Big Eight record by being nominated four times for Lineman-of-the-Week laurels.

In his junior year, Newton paved the way for sophomore Jeff Kinney to explode onto the scene. Kinney rushed for a team-high 619 yards and 10 touchdowns. On the year the Huskers rushed for 2,312 yards and 22 touchdowns.

Newton’s senior year he started on an offensive line that guided the Huskers to their first national championship. In the title game, the Huskers rushed for 132 yards and had 293 yards of total offense. On the season, Nebraska rushed for 3,012 yards which was 700 more yards than the previous year. The Husker line paved the way for four 300-yard rushers and two rushers that went over 600 yards on the year (Kinney – 699 yards and Joe Orduna – 915 yards). The Huskers were second in the conference in total yards with 421.3 yards per game, only 1.6 yards per game behind leader Colorado.

·         1971 Senior Bowl, Coaches All American game, 1971 College All Star Game

·         1970 First-Team All-American (AP, Coaches-Kodak, FWAA-Look, Football News, Central Press Captains)

·         1970 Second-Team All-American (NEA, UPI)

·         1970 First-Team All-Big 8 (AP, UPI)

·         1970 Nebraska Lineman-of-the-Week (Wake Forest, Minnesota, Kansas, Oklahoma State)

==Professional career==
Newton played for the [[Chicago Bears]] from 1971 to 1975 and with Pro Football Hall of Fame players [[Dick Butkus]], [[Gale Sayers]] and [[Walter Payton]]. He played for the [[Seattle Seahawks]] from 1976 to 1981 with Hall of Famer [[Steve Largent]]. Newton was on the 1976 [[Seattle Seahawks]] expansion team that got the franchise started. He was a third round draft selection of the Chicago Bears and was moved from offensive tackle to guard his rookie year. He was named 1980 Seahawks [[Lineman (American football)|Lineman]] of the Year. In 1983, Newton had brief playing experiences with the [[Boston Breakers]] and [[Chicago Blitz]] of the [[USFL]], but his chemical dependency illness forced him to leave both teams.<ref name="BlogTalkRadio tutor" />

==Post-football career==
In July 1983, Newton entered Valley General Hospital treatment center in [[Monroe, Washington]] for chemical dependency. After treatment he went back to the University of Nebraska to finish his education and in 1986, he began working in the chemical dependency field. He received his master's degree from Capella University in 2005. He has over 30 years experience as a counselor, educator, administrator and professional speaker. Newton previously worked for the Betty Ford center for many years as lead counselor and director. He also served as lead relapse prevention facilitator for the Young Adult Track at the [[Betty Ford Center]].<ref name="BlogTalkRadio tutor" />

Today, Bob works as an independent consultant. He provides counseling and administrative services in communities struggling with substance abuse. 

''"I work with patients in privates clinics and outpatient settings ... We have a real problem with substance use disorders and addictive drugs in our society ... helping patients get well can be very rewarding."''

He is also in the HOF of [[Beta Theta Pi]] fraternity.[http://www.betathetapi.org/dmdocuments/beta-quick-facts.pdf Beta Theta Pi] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090226013641/http://www.betathetapi.org/dmdocuments/beta-quick-facts.pdf |date=February 26, 2009 }} He is a member of the Missouri Sports Hall of Fame Honor Roll of World Champions for the 1969 Chiefs team. In 2009, Stein conceived and began the first [[class action]] lawsuit on behalf of retired NFL players against the NFL. His case, ''Dryer v. NFL'', fought for fair payment for the NFL's use of player identities, including in NFL Films. He represents many past NFL players in concussion-related cases. '''Robert Charles McKay''' (born December 27, 1947) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive lineman]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1970 through 1978 with the [[Cleveland Browns]] and [[New England Patriots]].

As a college player at the [[University of Texas]], McKay earned consensus All-American honors during the 1969 season, helping Texas win the national championship.<ref>{{cite book |last=Canning |first=Whit |title=Where Have You Gone: James Street, Charles Gilbert, Roosevelt Leaks, and other Texas Greats |location=Champaign, Illinois |publisher=Sports Publishing LLC |year=2005 }}</ref>

During a 1975 [[Cleveland Stadium|Browns home game]] against the [[Browns-Steelers rivalry|rival]] [[1975 Pittsburgh Steelers season|Pittsburgh Steelers]], [[Joe Greene]] repeatedly [[kick]]ed McKay in the [[groin]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.morningjournal.com/articles/2008/09/14/sports/doc48cc8d241031f428316969.txt |title=Rivalry makes turn to primetime - morningjournal.com |access-date=2012-02-18 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120218215807/http://www.morningjournal.com/articles/2008/09/14/sports/doc48cc8d241031f428316969.txt |archive-date=2012-02-18 }}</ref> Greene was soon wrestled to the ground and punched by center [[Tom DeLeone]] and tight end [[Gary Parris]], allowing McKay to throw several haymakers on Greene before referees restored order.

'''Robert Kenneth Kuberski Jr.''' (born April 5, 1971) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Green Bay Packers]] and the [[New England Patriots]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Navy Midshipmen football|Navy Midshipmen]].

==Biography==
Kuberski graduated from [[Ridley High School]] in 1989 and attended the [[United States Naval Academy]] (Navy), where he was a three-year [[Varsity letter|letter]] winner and a two-time all-East selection.

Kuberski was selected by the Packers in the seventh round (183rd overall) of the [[1993 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1993 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1993/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Bembry |first1=Jerry |title=Kuberski draft, but left in cold Packers must wait for Navy lineman |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/news/bs-xpm-1993-04-27-1993117086-story.html |work=The Baltimore Sun |accessdate=19 May 2020}}</ref> He served on active duty as an Ensign in the United States Navy for two years prior to the beginning of his NFL career.

He played in Green Bay for four seasons from 1995 to 1998, seeing action in forty-nine games in which he also served as Green Bay's representative to the [[National Football League Players Association|NFL Players Association]] for 1996–1998. In [[1999 NFL season|1999]], he signed with the New England Patriots, closed out his career playing in five games. Kuberski had two career sacks.<ref>{{cite web |title=Kuberski's Time in Green Bay Turned Out to be a Solid Investment |url=https://www.packers.com/news/kuberski-s-time-in-green-bay-turned-out-to-be-a-solid-investment-2451090 |website=www.packers.com |accessdate=19 May 2020}}</ref>

In 2009, he was selected to the Navy Marine Corps Memorial All-Stadium Defensive Line. A member of the Navy Sports Hall of Fame, he was inducted into the [[Pennsylvania Sports Hall of Fame]] in 2016. He remains active in the Naval Academy community via his involvement as a Trustee of the United States Naval Academy Foundation and serves as President of the Class of 1993.

Kuberski got his start in financial services as an off-season intern at Associated Investments following his rookie year in Green Bay. He then spent ten years as a regional vice president at Invesco after working as a financial advisor at [[Morgan Stanley]]. The head of global relationship management at Eaton Vance (Morgan Stanley) and then of retail sales at RidgeWorth Investments (Virtus), he subsequently became the head of Wealth Management Consulting Group at [[Cohen & Steers]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Robert Kuberski '93 |url=https://www.usna.com/about/bot-kuberski |website=www.usna.com |accessdate=19 May 2020}}</ref>

'''Robert William Nelson''' (born March 3, 1959) is a retired [[American football]] [[nose tackle]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played for the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] for one season and the [[Green Bay Packers]] for two seasons. Prior to entering the NFL, Nelson had a stint with the [[Arizona Outlaws]] of the [[United States Football League|USFL]].  Nelson played [[college football]] at the [[University of Miami|University of Miami (Florida)]].

Nelson gained a bit of fame in the early 1990s through his inclusion in the Nintendo home video game "[[Tecmo Super Bowl]]."  Nelson was among the most dominant defensive players in the game, even though he played as a [[nose tackle]], a position in which the primary responsibility is to occupy [[offensive lineman|offensive linemen]] to allow other defensive players to make tackles.  Nelson's speed in the game enabled him to make a [[quarterback sack|sack]] on nearly every play as a human-controlled player.  As a result, players of Tecmo Super Bowl frequently agree not to use the play.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kaduk |first=Kevin |date=October 17, 2021 |title=30 NFL legends who were awesome in Tecmo Super Bowl |url=https://thelistwire.usatoday.com/lists/nfl-legends-tecmo-super-bowl-30th-anniversary-nintendo/ |access-date=October 13, 2023 |website=List Wire|publisher=USA Today |quote=The real-life Nelson had three sacks in three years as the Packers’ nose tackle. The video game Nelson was an inexplainable, unstoppable force whose use is often legislated out of play because of the unfairness of it all.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Secret 'Tecmo' assassins |url=https://journalstar.com/secret-tecmo-assassins/article_b04b97f9-95fd-55a1-9c99-9af36700c6bc.html |website=JournalStar.com |access-date=October 13, 2023 |date=January 25, 2012 |quote=Nelson was a nose tackle who, because of a ratings error, was given unnatural acceleration ability. Coupled with his position, this made him king of the typically outlawed "Nose Tackle Dive," in which your nose tackle makes a slight move and dives, instantly sacking the quarterback on most pass plays.}}</ref>

'''Robert Alan McCaffrey''' (born April 16, 1952) is a former [[National Football League]] (NFL) [[Center (American football)|center]] who had a notable career while a [[student athlete]] on the [[University of Southern California]] (USC) [[USC Trojans football|Trojans football team]].

After playing football at [[Garces Memorial High School]] in Bakersfield, California, McCaffrey played football at the University of Southern California where he lettered three seasons, 1972–74.  The Trojans won [[NCAA Division I FBS National Football Championship|national championships]] and played in the [[Rose Bowl (game)|Rose Bowl]] in 1972 and 1974.  He was honored as USC's Lineman of the Year in 1974 and junior varsity MVP in 1971. He played in the 1975 [[Chicago Charities College All-Star Game]] where a team of star college seniors played the [[Super Bowl IX]] champion [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], losing 21–14.<ref name=BrentBio>[http://usctrojans.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/mccaffrey_brent00.html Player Bio: Brent McCaffrey] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307194405/http://www.usctrojans.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/mccaffrey_brent00.html |date=2016-03-07 }}, USC Trojans Athletic Department, accessed October 21, 2008.</ref>  He graduated from USC in 1975.<ref name=TFM04>[http://uprserver4.usc.edu/trojan_family/winter04/ClassNotes.html Class Notes] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720101837/http://uprserver4.usc.edu/trojan_family/winter04/ClassNotes.html |date=2011-07-20 }}, ''Trojan Family Magazine'', Winter 2004, accessed October 21, 2008.

</ref>

==Professional career==
McCaffrey was drafted by the [[Green Bay Packers]] in the [[1975 NFL draft]]<ref>[https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/McCaBo20.htm Bob McCaffrey], Pro-Football-Reference.com</ref> and played one season before retiring.

==Personal==
The son of McCaffrey and wife Karen, Brent McCaffrey, played football for USC as a [[left tackle]], lettering for three seasons (1998–2000).<ref name="BrentBio"/>

==After football==
McCaffrey joined his father-in-law, John Bonadelle, and became real estate developer in [[Fresno, California]]. He now heads The McCaffrey Group and is on the board of directors of the Building Industry Association of Fresno/Madera Counties, having previously served as chairman of the board.<ref name="TFM04"/>{{dead link|date=December 2014}}

'''Robert N. M.''' "'''Blade'''" '''Thornbladh''' (born September 19, 1952) is an American former [[American football|football]] player, coach and radio color commentator.  He played professionally as a [[linebacker]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL)

Thornbladh played [[college football]] for the [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan Wolverines]] team from 1971 to 1973 and was an assistant coach at Michigan from 1980 to 1986.  He later served as the color commentator for Michigan football broadcasts on [[WJR]] radio.

==Playing career==
Thornbladh was born in [[Cleveland, Ohio]], in 1952 and graduated from Plymouth High School in [[Plymouth, Michigan]].<ref name=DB>{{cite web|title=Bob Thornbladh player profile |publisher=databasefootball |url=http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=THORNBOB01 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110610062448/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=THORNBOB01 |archive-date=2011-06-10 }}</ref>  He enrolled at the [[University of Michigan]] in 1970 and played at the [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] position for the [[Michigan Wolverines football|Wolverines]] from 1971 to 1973.<ref>{{cite news|title=U-M Coach Glad He Kept Thornbladh at Fullback|newspaper=Ironwood Daily Globe|date=1972-11-16}}</ref>  He gained 677 rushing yards for the Wolverines on 163 carries for an average of 4.2 yards per carry.  He scored 11 rushing touchdowns, and his longest run for Michigan was a 31-yard gain against Wisconsin in 1973.  Thornbladh also had seven pass receptions for Michigan, gaining 55 yards for an average of 7.9 yards per reception.  He also returned five kickoffs for 52 yards for an average of 10.4 yards per return.<ref>{{cite web|title=Michigan Football Statistic Archive Query Page |publisher=University of Michigan |url=http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071112175906/http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |archive-date=2007-11-12 }}</ref>

Thornbladh was selected by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the 11th round of the [[1974 NFL draft]] (275th overall pick).<ref name=DB/>  He made the Chiefs' regular season roster in the [[1974 NFL season]] as a backup to middle linebacker [[Willie Lanier]], but he played only on the special teams
in 14 regular season games.<ref name=KC>{{cite news|title=Chiefs deal Thornbladh|newspaper=The Argus, Fremont - Newark, Calif. (UPI story)|date=1975-07-17}}</ref>  In July 1975, the Chiefs traded Thornbladh to the [[Detroit Lions]] for an undisclosed future draft choice.<ref name=KC/>  The Lions placed Thornbladh on waivers in August 1975.<ref>{{cite news|title=Lions Contract Landry, Laslavic|newspaper=Pacific Stars and Stripes|date=1975-08-09}}</ref>

==Coaching career==
In 1976, Thornbladh returned to the University of Michigan as a graduate assistant on Bo Schembechler's coaching staff.  In 1976, Thornbladh accompanied the team to the Rose Bowl and was the subject of an [[Associated Press]] story about expensive soup. Thornbladh was sent by Schembechler to get 15 tuna fish sandwiches and {{not a typo|15 cups}} of soup for the coaching staff.  Thornbladh placed the order at a nearby restaurant and came back later to pick it up.  The bill came to $50.56, and Thornbladh did not have enough money.  In order to avoid losing the entire sale, the restaurant agreed to sell him the 15 sandwiches without soup for $28.  After hearing the story, Schembechler sent him back to the restaurant the next day to buy a single order of soup, wanting to find out how "$2 soup-to-go" tastes.<ref>{{cite news|title=Cost of soup ($2) leaves Bo short-changed|newspaper=Anderson Daily Bulletin|date=1976-12-27}}</ref>

In 1980, Thornbladh was promoted to assistant coach at Michigan, a position that he held until 1986.

===Later years and family===
After retiring from coaching, Thornbladh became the color commentator on [[WJR]] radio broadcasts of Michigan Wolverines football games.<ref>{{cite news|author=Jack Berry|title=U-M Broadcaster Begs to Differ with Bo|newspaper=The Detroit News and Detroit Free Press|date=1990-01-01}}</ref>
